answer: Under section 108(1) of the Employment Rights Act 1996, section 94 does not apply to the dismissal of an employee unless he has been continuously employed for a period of not less than two years ending with the effective date of termination. However, under section 108(2), if an employee is dismissed by reason of any requirement or recommendation referred to in section 64(2), the qualifying period is substituted with one month. Additionally, subsection (1) does not apply if the reason (or, if more than one, the principal reason) for the dismissal is, or relates to, the employee's political opinions or affiliation. It also does not apply if the reason (or, if more than one, the principal reason) for the dismissal is, or is connected with, the employee's membership of a reserve force (as defined in section 374 of the Armed Forces Act 2006), or if any of the provisions specified in subsection (3) apply.

answer: Under section 98(1) and (2) of the Employment Rights Act 1996, to show a fair reason for dismissal, the employer must establish that the reason relates to the capability or qualifications of the employee, relates to the conduct of the employee, is that the employee was redundant, involves a statutory restriction under subsection (2)(d), or is some other substantial reason justifying dismissal. Capability is assessed by reference to skill, aptitude, health, or any other physical or mental quality under section 98(3)(a). Once the employer fulfills these requirements, section 98(4) provides that whether the dismissal is fair or unfair depends on whether in the circumstances, including the size and administrative resources of the employer’s undertaking, the employer acted reasonably or unreasonably in treating that reason as sufficient, determined in accordance with equity and the substantial merits of the case.

answer: Under section 113 of the Employment Rights Act 1996, a tribunal may decide to make an order for reinstatement in accordance with section 114 or an order for re-engagement in accordance with section 115. An order for reinstatement requires the employer to treat the complainant in all respects as if he had not been dismissed, whereas an order for re-engagement orders that the complainant be engaged by the employer, a successor, or an associated employer in comparable or other suitable employment. When making either order, the tribunal must specify the date for compliance, any rights and privileges to be restored, and any amount payable by the employer for benefits and arrears of pay, subject to reductions for certain sums received by the complainant.

answer: Under regulation 13(1) of The Working Time Regulations 1998, a worker is entitled to four weeks' annual leave in each leave year, subject to regulation 13(5). In addition, under regulation 13A(1) and (2)(e), a worker is entitled to 1.6 weeks of additional leave in any leave year beginning on or after 1st April 2009. The aggregate entitlement under regulation 13(1) and regulation 13A(2) is subject to a maximum of 28 days. Under regulation 13(9)(b), leave to which a worker is entitled under regulation 13 may not be replaced by a payment in lieu except where the worker’s employment is terminated. Under regulation 13A(6), leave to which a worker is entitled under regulation 13A may not be replaced by a payment in lieu except where the worker’s employment is terminated, the leave is an entitlement that arises under paragraph (2)(a), (b) or (c), or the leave is an entitlement to 0.8 weeks that arises under paragraph (2)(d) in respect of that part of the leave year which would have elapsed before 1st April 2009. Under regulations 13(5) and 13A(5), if the date on which a worker’s employment begins is later than the date on which the first leave year begins, the leave entitlement is a proportion equal to the proportion of that leave year remaining on the date employment begins.

Furthermore, under section 27(1), a purchaser of a legal estate from trustees of land is not concerned with the trusts affecting the land, the net income of the land, or the proceeds of sale. Under section 2(2), where the trustees are two or more individuals approved or appointed by the court (or their successors in office), or a trust corporation, any equitable interest or power having priority to the trust is overreached and attaches instead to the proceeds of sale and income of the land, subject to the exceptions listed in section 2(3).

answer: Under section 84(1) of the Law of Property Act 1925, the Upper Tribunal has the power, on the application of any person interested in freehold land affected by a restriction, to wholly or partially discharge or modify the restriction by order. To do so, the Tribunal must be satisfied that the restriction ought to be deemed obsolete, that its continuation would impede reasonable user of the land under subsection (1A), that those entitled to its benefit have agreed to the discharge or modification, or that the proposal will not injure those entitled to the benefit. Under section 84(1A), subsection (1)(aa) authorises the discharge or modification where the Upper Tribunal is satisfied that the restriction does not secure to persons entitled to the benefit of it any practical benefits of substantial value or advantage to them, or is contrary to the public interest, and that money will be an adequate compensation for any loss or disadvantage suffered. In determining whether a restriction ought to be discharged or modified, section 84(1B) requires the Upper Tribunal to take into account the development plan, any declared or ascertainable pattern for the grant or refusal of planning permissions in the relevant areas, the period at which and context in which the restriction was created or imposed, and any other material circumstances.

answer: Under section 3(1) of the Party Wall etc. Act 1996, before exercising any right conferred by section 2, a building owner must serve a "party structure notice" on any adjoining owner stating the building owner's name and address, the nature and particulars of the proposed work, and the date the work will begin. Where the building owner proposes to construct special foundations, section 3(1)(b) requires the notice to also include plans, sections, and details of construction together with reasonable particulars of the loads to be carried thereby. According to section 3(2)(b), the notice ceases to have effect if the work to which it relates has not begun within the period of twelve months beginning with the day on which the notice is served and is not prosecuted with due diligence. answer: Under section 3(1) of the Landlord and Tenant (Covenants) Act 1995, the benefit and burden of all landlord and tenant covenants of a tenancy are annexed and incident to the demised premises and the reversion, and pass on an assignment of the whole or any part of those premises or the reversion. When a tenant assigns, section 3(2) provides that the assignee becomes bound by the tenant covenants and entitled to the benefit of the landlord covenants, subject to specified exceptions regarding covenants not binding the assignor immediately beforehand or relating to premises not comprised in the assignment. Similarly, under section 3(3), an assignee of the landlord becomes bound by the landlord covenants and entitled to the benefit of the tenant covenants, subject to parallel exceptions. However, under section 3(6), covenants expressed to be personal do not become enforceable by or against another person, nor does the section make a covenant enforceable if it is unenforceable due to non-registration under the Land Registration Act 2002 or the Land Charges Act 1972.

Under section 260(3), such a claim may be brought only in respect of a cause of action arising from an actual or proposed act or omission involving negligence, default, breach of duty or breach of trust by a director of the company, and the cause of action may be against the director, another person, or both. For these purposes, section 260(5) provides that a "director" includes a former director and a shadow director is treated as a director, while references to a member include a person to whom shares have been transferred or transmitted by operation of law. Furthermore, section 260(4) states that it is immaterial whether the cause of action arose before or after the person became a member of the company.

Section 830(3) notes that this definition has effect subject to sections 832, 833A and 835 (investment companies and Solvency 2 insurance companies).

answer: Under section 678(1) of the Companies Act 2006, where a person is acquiring or proposing to acquire shares in a public company, it is not lawful for that company, or a subsidiary of that company, to give financial assistance directly or indirectly for the purpose of the acquisition before or at the same time as the acquisition takes place. Under section 24(1), the right to a price reduction is the right to require the trader to reduce by an appropriate amount the price the consumer is required to pay under the contract, or anything else the consumer is required to transfer under the contract, and to receive a refund from the trader for anything already paid or otherwise transferred by the consumer above the reduced amount. According to section 24(2), the amount of the reduction may, where appropriate, be the full amount of the price or whatever the consumer is required to transfer. If the consumer instead exercises the final right to reject, section 24(8) provides that any refund may be reduced by a deduction for use, although under section 24(10) no deduction may be made in the first 6 months unless the goods consist of a motor vehicle or are specified by order made by the Secretary of State.
